To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) youths with greater negative mood symptoms had lower expression of GR and β2AR, 2) this effect was potentiated by greater average levels of depressive symptoms in the family, such that youths in families with greater levels of depressive symptoms experienced the greatest decrease in expression of GR and B2AR, and 3) this pattern was observed only in the context of the family environment.

coming from a family with more depressive symptoms on-average was associated with lower levels of expression of two genes relevant to asthma (GR and β2- AR) during times when youths experienced negative mood symptoms.

coming from a family with greater levels of depressive symptoms was associated with lower levels of gene expression in youths with asthma, and this effect was potentiated by the presence of negative mood symptoms in youths.
In summary, our research is concerned with

identifying the mechanisms by which parental depressive symptoms may potentiate the negative effects of child negative mood symptoms on biological processes that are relevant to disease pathology in children.
the identification of biological pathways through which depressive symptoms may influence pediatric asthma, and the results of this study provide evidence of one such mechanism.

understanding the role of depressive symptoms and negative mood symptoms on gene expression in youths with asthma, and how this relationship may vary based on the level of depressive symptoms within the family environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the combination of higher average parental depressive symptoms with greater child negative mood symptoms is associated with lower gene expression of GR and β2AR in children with asthma.
the current study identified novel and biologically proximal molecular signaling patterns in the GR and β2AR genes that connect depressive symptoms and asthma in children.

the current study provides evidence that coming from a family with more average levels of parental depression may potentiate the effect of negative mood on gene expression in children with asthma, such that children with greater negative mood symptoms who come from families with more average depressive symptoms may express the lowest levels of the two genes that are the primary molecular targets for asthma medications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

children with asthma who are experiencing more negative mood symptoms in the context of higher levels of depressive symptoms in their families may be more likely to express less of the receptor genes relevant to the effectiveness of asthma medication.
coming from a family with more depressive symptoms on a day-to-day basis may potentiate the effect of youths’ own negative moods on their asthma symptoms.

coming from a family with more depressive symptoms is associated with greater disease comorbidity and that these processes are mediated by molecular signaling processes that are relevant to the disease process.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the combination of greater parental depressive symptomatology and greater negative mood in children may be a particularly potent combination for understanding how depressive symptoms relate to disease-related outcomes.
the combination of a child experiencing more negative mood and coming from a family with more depressive symptoms is associated with lower expression of genes that regulate asthma symptoms.

coming from a family where parents have higher depressive symptoms can potentiate the effects that negative mood symptoms in the child has on the expression of the two receptor genes that are the primary target of asthma medications.
